options: The force of gravity pulling on an object's mass
How much space an object takes up
The amount of matter inside an object
questions.explanation: Weight is a force — gravity's pull on the object's mass — and is measured in newtons.
questions.misconception: Weight and mass are frequently merged into one idea; weight is the force (N), mass is the matter (kg).

questions.prompt: A 5 kg mass sits on Earth where g ≈ 10 m/s². What is its weight?
questions.misconception: Some pick 5 N (as if weight were the same number as mass) or 0.5 N (dividing) — the formula multiplies by g.

questions.prompt: The Moon's gravity is about 1/6 of Earth's. A 60 kg astronaut's weight on the Moon is roughly...
options: One sixth of their Earth weight
Exactly the same as on Earth
questions.explanation: Weight = mass × g; g is about 1/6 as large, so the force (weight) drops to about a sixth while the 60 kg mass is unchanged.
questions.misconception: Choosing 'same as Earth' conflates weight with mass; choosing 'zero' confuses orbit with the lunar surface (where gravity still pulls).

questions.prompt: Which unit is used to measure weight?
questions.explanation: Weight is a force, so it uses the newton (N). The kilogram measures mass, not the force.
questions.misconception: Everyday scales print kg, which hides the distinction — but weight is a force and its proper unit is the newton.

questions.prompt: An object moves from Earth to the Moon. Which statement is true?
options: Its mass stays the same, but its weight decreases
Its weight stays the same, but its mass increases
Both its mass and weight stay the same
Both its mass and weight decrease equally
questions.explanation: Mass is a property of the object and stays 60 kg; weight is gravitational pull and falls to about a sixth because g is smaller on the Moon.
questions.misconception: Swapping the roles (weight constant, mass changing) is the classic inversion of the two quantities.
